Well-Being Ring / Well-Being Design Series / Episode 04

The Guiding Light.

Every new feature makes a calm screen less calm.

This episode sets the rules the design follows: how people group what matters, six principles, a four-step support ladder, and the limits the app works within.

01  Card sorting

How people group what matters.

(Method: open card sort, planned with 5 to 8 people who feel stressed regularly; results to follow)

Participants receive 21 feature cards without predefined categories. They sort the cards into groups and name each group, which shows how people expect the app to be organised.

02  Design principles

Six rules the design follows.

(Source: project design principles, applied across the prototype)

Each rule has a reason. The line at the bottom of each card says what the rule stops from happening.

01

Decide for me

One clear action per state, never a menu.

Prevents: a menu at the worst moment.

02

No work from the user

The ring senses stress, so there is no mood logging.

Prevents: asking a drained person to do more.

03

Explain why

A "why the ring thinks this" card shows what the ring saw.

Prevents: a call the user has no reason to trust.

04

Calm by default

The home screen stays quiet, and depth lives one tap away in Insights.

Prevents: a home screen that grows with every feature.

05

Escalate safely

AI companion, then counselor, then doctor, then emergency help, with consent at each step.

Prevents: being stuck at the wrong level of help.

06

Never add pressure

Soft language, a Calm comfort setting for tone, and no alarming alerts.

Prevents: adding stress to someone who already has too much.

03  Escalation ladder

Four steps, each with consent.

(Source: Support tab of the prototype)

The app moves up only when the user needs more help. Anything shared at a step is shared only with consent.

  1. 1

    AI companion

    Available instantly and labelled as a supportive companion, not a therapist. It hands off to a human when distress is high.

  2. 2

    Real counselor

    Live availability or a booked slot. The user chooses what to share, with a live preview of what the counselor will see.

  3. 3

    Doctor

    In-person or video. A "share my stress summary" toggle, opt-in and revocable.

  4. 4

    Emergency help

    A helpline, a trusted contact, or a text chat, pinned at the bottom of Support.

04  Ethics and safety

Limits we design within.

(Source: project ethics and safety notes)

These limits shape the wording, the sharing controls and the crisis paths.

  1. 01

    Supports wellbeing, doesn't diagnose

    Well-Being Ring is not a medical device, and the app never presents a diagnosis.

  2. 02

    Measures the body, not feelings

    A ring detects physiological activation, not emotions, so the wording never claims to know how someone feels.

  3. 03

    The AI companion is labelled

    It is clearly labelled and hands off to a human when distress is high.

  4. 04

    Sharing is opt-in

    Sharing with counselors and doctors is opt-in, item by item, and can be revoked.

  5. 05

    Wellness advice only

    Food and sleep guidance is general wellness advice, not medical advice.

  6. 06

    Crisis paths need a professional

    Before any real launch, the crisis paths are tested with a mental health professional.

What this means for the screens. Every screen in Episode 05 follows these rules: one clear action, a reason for it, and nothing that adds pressure.
